A right shift moves each element to the right by 1 (circular). Equivalent to rotating array left by k? Let's define: Right shift (as described) shifts each element to the right, i.e., after one right shift, element originally at index i moves to index (i+1)%n, which means array becomes [last element, first, second, ..., second-last]. That is a rotation to the right by 1 (i.e., moving the last element to front). So new[0] = old[n-1]; new[1] = old[0]; ... new[n-1] = old[n-2]. That's a rotation of the array to the right by 1 (last becomes first). Yes.

Thus performing k right shifts yields rotation to the right by k (i.e., move last k elements to front, preserving order). So after k shifts, array = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k] (with k modulo n). Need to find minimal k (0 <= k < n) such that rotated array is sorted ascending.

But we can do O(n) by finding the number of "breaks" where nums[i] > nums[(i+1)%n]. For a sorted rotated array (ascending), there should be at most one such break. Actually for a strictly increasing sorted array (no duplicates) rotated, there will be exactly one place where nums[i] > nums[(i+1)%n] if it is rotated (not already sorted). If already sorted (no rotation), there will be zero such breaks. If more than one break, impossible to sort by rotations.

Thus count breaks. If count == 0 => answer 0. If count == 1 => we need to rotate such that element after break becomes first? Let's derive.
